title: Would You Rather?
purpose: Choose between two options, then try to convince a partner. The reason matters more than the choice.
setup: Put up a question. Students can raise a hand, point to a side or move across the room. Use the vote buttons if you want to record the class totals.
steps: Give an example
Read the first question and give your own answer with a reason. Let students think for a moment before they choose.
Compare answers
In pairs, both students explain their choice. Ask them to follow up with “Why?” or “What about…?” Try a second question with a new partner.
Try to change a mind
Put up another question. In groups of four, students explain their choices and respond to each other. They can change sides if someone makes a good point.
Take a few answers
Hear two or three reasons from the room. Ask everyone to tell a partner which reason they found most convincing.
frames: “I’d rather ___ because ___.” · “Why would you choose ___?”
skills: Giving opinions · Using because · Asking follow-up questions
support: Use “I choose ___ because it is fun / useful / easier.”
stretch: Ask them to find a drawback to their own choice.

rounds.title: Would you rather have…
options: An extra hour of free time every day

note: If everyone picks the same side, ask them to make the best case for the other one.

title: Rank It
purpose: Give each group a list to put in order. They have to agree, which gives them something to discuss.
setup: Show the list. Groups make their own ranking on paper. Use the arrows on the board when you want to compare a group’s answer with the class.
steps: Set the situation
Read the question and check any unfamiliar words. Each student chooses what they would put first.
Hear everyone’s choice
Go round the group. Each person names their top item and explains why. Encourage the others to ask questions.
Agree on one list
Groups write a shared ranking. Everyone should suggest a change or give a reason. Ask them to explain their first and last choices.
Compare the lists
Hear from a few groups. Where the rankings differ, ask students to explain why they made a different choice.
frames: “___ is more useful than ___ because ___.” · “I disagree because ___.”
skills: Comparing things · Agreeing and disagreeing · Explaining choices
support: Use four items instead of six.
stretch: Change the situation and ask whether their ranking still works.

rounds.title: Stranded on an island: most useful first.
A new school: which improvement matters most?
A long train journey: what would you pack first?

note: There is no answer sheet here. A sensible reason is enough, even if another group disagrees.

title: Find Someone Who…
purpose: Students move around asking short questions and finding things out about their classmates.
setup: Show the prompts. Students copy short labels and leave space for names. If there isn’t room to move, change partners at their desks.
steps: Show how to ask
Turn “likes spicy food” into “Do you like spicy food?” Model a yes/no answer and one follow-up question.
Find a few people
Students ask different classmates and note a name for each yes. They need to hear the answer before writing it down.
Find out a bit more
Keep going with new partners. Ask students to add a follow-up, such as “What do you draw?” They should remember one detail about someone.
Tell a partner
Each student shares two things they found out. Take a few examples from the class if there is time.
frames: “Do you like ___?” · “Can you ___?” · “What kind of ___?”
skills: Forming questions · Listening for details · Talking about another person
support: Write the full questions beside the prompts.
stretch: Use a different name for every prompt and ask two follow-up questions.

rounds.title: A few things we have in common
Ask about favourites
items: Likes the same colour as you
Enjoys the same food as you
Likes the same season as you
Enjoys the same school subject as you
Likes the same kind of music as you

note: Keep an ear out for students reading the prompt instead of asking a question. Model the question again and let them try.

title: Describe & Draw
purpose: One student describes a hidden picture. Their partner draws what they hear. Compare the results, then swap.
setup: Pairs need paper and pencils. Let the describers read the secret scene while the drawers face away. Hide it before they turn back. The drawing pad is useful for a class example.
steps: Make the task clear
Model “Draw a circle above a square.” Explain that the describer can talk, but can’t point at the partner’s paper.
Describe and draw
Show scene A to the describers, then hide it. They describe the scene while their partners draw and ask questions. Reveal it to compare.
Swap roles
Use scene B. The new describer gives the instructions. Ask pairs to notice which words made the second drawing easier to follow.
Compare what happened
Each pair shares one helpful instruction or one misunderstanding. Put a useful phrase on the board for next time.
frames: “Draw ___ next to ___.” · “On the left or the right?” · “Could you repeat that?”
skills: Position words · Describing size and number · Asking for clarification
support: Start with three objects. Check above, below, left and right first.
stretch: Ask the describer to add sizes, colours or extra details.

rounds.title: Secret scene A
rounds.answer: A house; a tree on the left; a cat on the roof; three flowers in front.

rounds.title: Secret scene B
rounds.answer: A boat; a fish below it; a sun above it; a bird on the right.

rounds.title: Secret scene C
rounds.answer: A robot in the middle; a hat on its head; a ball by its left foot; two stars above it.

note: The drawing doesn’t have to be good. If the cat ends up under the house, work out which instruction led to it.

title: Mystery Object
purpose: Give an ordinary object a new purpose. Groups decide what it does and explain how someone would use it.
setup: Bring a small object, such as a binder clip or an empty box. If you don’t have one, use the name on the page. The extra challenge gives students a particular person to design for.
steps: Describe the object
Show it and collect a few words about its shape, material and size. Ask what else it could be used for.
Come up with ideas
Each student suggests a use. The group asks how the ideas would work and chooses one to develop.
Explain the invention
Give it a name and prepare a short explanation. Everyone contributes a line about what it does or how to use it.
Share with another group
Groups explain their ideas to their neighbours. Ask the listeners which part they would like to try.
frames: “It might be ___.” · “It could help you ___.” · “We think it is used for ___.”
skills: Describing objects · Using could and might · Explaining a use
support: Offer a few words: metal, plastic, round, hold, carry, open.
stretch: Ask what could go wrong with the invention and how to fix it.

rounds.title: A binder clip
rounds.answer: Find a new use for it on a camping trip.

rounds.title: A kitchen whisk
rounds.answer: Give it a use outside the kitchen.

rounds.title: A rubber band
rounds.answer: Use it to solve a small problem at school.

rounds.title: An empty box
rounds.answer: Make something useful for a crowded desk.

note: Once someone says the real name of the object, move straight to inventing another use for it.

title: Two Truths and a Lie
purpose: Students write three statements about themselves. Classmates ask questions before guessing which one is made up.
setup: Choose a topic such as food, hobbies or school. The statements on the page are examples to replace. Students can use an invented character if they prefer.
steps: Play one round together
Give three statements of your own: two true, one invented. Let the class ask a question before guessing.
Write three statements
Students write their own. Help them phrase anything they’re unsure about and give them time to practise saying it.
Ask, then guess
Take turns in groups. Each person reads their statements. The others ask questions, make a guess, and hear the answer.
Remember something true
Students tell a partner one true thing they learnt. Ask for a few examples of questions that helped.
frames: “How often do you ___?” · “When did you ___?” · “I think ___ is the lie because ___.”
skills: Writing short statements · Asking questions · Listening for clues
support: Start with “I like…”, “I can…” and “I have…”
stretch: Use past experiences and ask two questions before guessing.

rounds.title: Food
items: I put ketchup on ice cream.
I eat an apple every day.

rounds.title: Hobbies
items: I can play a musical instrument.

note: Don’t let it become three statements followed by an instant guess. The questions are the useful part.

title: Taboo Lite
purpose: Explain a word without saying the obvious clues. Useful practice for when students know what they mean but can’t find a word.
setup: Only the clue-giver should see the card. Keep the guessers facing away from the screen. For several groups at once, copy a few cards onto paper.
steps: Give a quick example
For pizza, try “It is usually round. You cut it into slices.” Explain that they can’t say the target word, the banned words or a translation.
Play a few turns
Give each clue-giver up to a minute. The others guess. Change the clue-giver after every word so everyone has a turn.
Make new cards
Each student writes a familiar word and two words the clue-giver can’t use. Shuffle and play another round.
Collect useful clues
Ask which descriptions worked. Choose a difficult word and see whether the class can explain it another way.
frames: “It is a kind of ___.” · “You use it to ___.” · “It is similar to ___.”
skills: Explaining vocabulary · Describing a function · Listening for meaning
support: Ban just one word and allow a pass after an attempt.
stretch: Ban three words or ask for a second description of the same word.
note: If the word itself is unfamiliar, change it. The point is finding another way to say something.

title: Picture Story
purpose: Three pictures, one short story. Groups find a way to connect them and tell it in about a minute.
setup: Show the three pictures and check the names. Groups can use paper for a few notes, but don’t need to write out the whole story.
steps: Start them off
Name the pictures and give a possible opening sentence. Leave the rest of the story to them.
Put a story together
Each person suggests something that happens. Groups agree on a beginning, a problem and an ending that use all three pictures.
Practise telling it
Give everyone a line. Rehearse once and keep it to about a minute. If it’s too long, decide which parts they can leave out.
Tell another group
Neighbouring groups tell each other their stories. Listeners say which part they liked and ask a question.
frames: “First, ___.” · “Then, ___.” · “Suddenly, ___!” · “Finally, ___.”
skills: Putting events in order · Telling a story · Linking ideas
support: Use three sentences starting with first, then and finally.
stretch: Add a line of dialogue and an unexpected ending.

rounds.title: Connect all three in one story.
Connect all three in one story.
Connect all three in one story.
Connect all three in one story.

note: Let the story be a bit ridiculous. They still need to make the connection clear to the listener.

title: Sell Me This
purpose: Make a 30-second advertisement for something ordinary. Give people a reason to want it.
setup: Give each group a pencil, spoon, sock or notebook. They can use the object named on screen if you don’t have one. The extra customer is there if they need another angle.
steps: Show them the idea
Pick up an object and give a quick sales pitch. Invented features are fine, as long as students explain what they do.
Decide what to sell
Groups choose a name, a customer and two reasons to buy the product. Everyone suggests a benefit.
Rehearse the advert
Put the ideas into a 30-second advert. Give each student a line and practise saying it clearly.
Try it on an audience
Perform to a neighbouring group. Listeners say which feature would persuade them to buy it.
frames: “You need this because ___.” · “It is the most ___.” · “With this, you can ___.”
skills: Describing benefits · Using adjectives · Persuading a listener
support: Use a name, two features and “Try it today.”
stretch: Have the audience raise an objection for the sellers to answer.

rounds.title: Sell this: a pencil
rounds.answer: Your customer keeps losing their stationery.

rounds.title: Sell this: a spoon
rounds.answer: Your customer is going on a camping trip.

rounds.title: Sell this: a sock
rounds.answer: Your customer cycles to school in the rain.

rounds.title: Sell this: a notebook
rounds.answer: Your customer always forgets what they need to do.

note: A pencil is enough. The interest comes from what they claim it can do.

title: Mini Debate
purpose: Take a side on a school issue, prepare a couple of reasons and respond to someone who disagrees.
setup: Show one statement. Students choose a side. If almost everyone agrees, invite a few volunteers to argue the other case for practice.
steps: Choose a side
Read the statement and model a reason. Give them a polite way to disagree: “I see your point, but…”
Prepare two reasons
Students work with someone on the same side. Think of two reasons and a concrete example, then practise explaining them.
Discuss both sides
Join another pair, ideally with a different view. Take turns giving reasons and answering each other. Everyone asks or answers a question.
Reconsider
Ask which reason from the other side was strongest. Take another show of hands to see whether anyone changed their mind.
frames: “I agree because ___.” · “I see your point, but ___.” · “For example, ___.”
skills: Giving arguments · Disagreeing politely · Responding to a point
support: Give a reason to finish: “A later start would help because…”
stretch: Finish by agreeing on a compromise.

rounds.title: Students should choose their own seats.
Every school should have a garden.
A class trip is better than a class party.

note: One clear reason is better than a long list they can’t explain. Ask for an example.

title: Guess My Word
purpose: Ask yes/no questions to work out a hidden word. Start broad, then narrow it down.
setup: Turn the guesser away while the rest of the group reads the word. Hide it before they turn back. Use paper cards if several groups are playing at once.
steps: Model a few questions
Show how “Is it alive?” rules out several possibilities. Put “Is it…?”, “Can it…?” and “Do people…?” on the board.
Play and swap
Give each guesser up to ten questions or two minutes, then a final guess. Reveal the word and change the guesser.
Keep everyone involved
Continue until everyone has had a turn. Ask the group to notice which questions helped most. Add familiar words on paper if needed.
Keep the useful questions
Hear a good question from each group. Ask students to improve a question that didn’t give them much information.
frames: “Is it alive?” · “Can you eat it?” · “Do people use it at school?”
skills: Yes/no questions · Describing categories · Using answers to narrow a guess
support: Tell the guesser the category and leave question starters visible.
stretch: Try a six-question limit.
note: If they keep guessing individual words, stop briefly and model a question that rules out a whole category.

title: Odd One Out
purpose: Choose which word doesn’t belong and explain your rule. A different answer can be just as good.
setup: Show one set of four words. Tell students that they need a reason for their answer. Keep the suggested reasons hidden until they have discussed it.
steps: Give one answer
For dog, eagle, shark and tiger, try “Eagle, because it can fly.” Ask whether a different answer could work.
Find another reason
Students choose privately, then explain their answers in groups. Ask each group to find at least two answers it can defend.
Make a set
Try the next prompt. Then groups write four words of their own and swap with another group to discuss.
Hear the explanations
Take a few answers and ask which rule each group used. Partners choose the explanation they found clearest.
frames: “___ is different because ___.” · “The others all ___.” · “Another answer could be ___.”
skills: Grouping vocabulary · Giving reasons · Explaining a different view
support: Check the word meanings and offer “The others all…”
stretch: Find a reason for every word to be the odd one out.

rounds.title: Which is the odd one out?
rounds.answer: Eagle can fly; shark lives in water; dog is commonly kept as a pet. Other clear reasons can work too.

rounds.title: Which is the odd one out?
rounds.answer: Bicycle is powered by pedalling; boat travels on water; train follows rails. Defend a different answer if you can.

rounds.title: Which is the odd one out?
rounds.answer: Carrot is usually grouped as a vegetable; banana is normally peeled before eating; grapes often grow in bunches. Explain your rule.

note: Wait before revealing the examples. Once there’s an answer on the board, they may stop looking for their own.

title: One-Minute Expert
purpose: Give students a familiar topic and a little thinking time, then ask them to talk for up to a minute.
setup: Use a topic from the page. Students note a few words rather than a full script. Start with 30 seconds if a minute feels too long.
steps: Give a short example
Talk for 20 seconds using an opinion, a reason and an example. Point out how those three parts gave you something to say.
Prepare and try
Students write three keywords. Each gives a 30-second talk to a partner, who asks one question. Swap.
Have another go
Keep the topic or choose a new one. Change partners and aim for a slightly longer talk. Use the one-minute timer for turns.
Notice what helped
Partners name a clear idea they heard. Ask students which keyword or question helped them keep going.
frames: “I think ___ because ___.” · “For example, ___.” · “Another thing is ___.”
skills: Speaking at length · Organising ideas · Giving examples
support: Aim for 20–30 seconds and give three useful words.
stretch: Have the listener ask a question the speaker hasn’t prepared for.

rounds.title: A game you enjoy
items: Who would you recommend it to?

note: Allow pauses. The aim is to get a thought across without writing every sentence first.

title: Improve This
purpose: Start with an obviously bad school idea. Groups make three changes and explain why their version is better.
setup: Show one of the bad ideas. Groups need paper for their improvements. Use the extra condition only if they need more of a challenge.
steps: Find the problem
Read the idea and ask what would go wrong. Give one suggestion using “We should…”
Suggest changes
Each student offers a fix. Ask who it would help and how it would make a difference.
Agree on three fixes
Groups choose their best three changes. Prepare a short explanation, with a line or a reason from each person.
Compare versions
Groups explain their plans to their neighbours. Listeners choose the most useful change and say why.
frames: “We should ___.” · “Students could ___.” · “It would be better if ___.”
skills: Making suggestions · Using should and could · Explaining improvements
support: Give two possible changes and ask students to choose one.
stretch: Keep the extra condition and explain how the plan still works.

rounds.title: The cafeteria only serves plain rice, every day.
rounds.answer: Your improved menu must include one meal everyone can customise.

rounds.title: The library has no chairs and closes at break time.
rounds.answer: You can change only three things.

rounds.title: The school playground is one enormous car park.
rounds.answer: Your plan needs one quiet space and one active space.

note: Push beyond “make it better”. What exactly would they change?

title: Morning Poll
purpose: Take a quick class vote, discuss the choices, then use the results to practise comparisons.
setup: Read the question and count a show of hands. Enter the totals using the vote buttons. Students can also move to different parts of the room to choose.
steps: Take the vote
Check that everyone understands the options. Count one vote per person and leave the results hidden for now.
Explain the choices
Partners explain their votes and ask each other a question. Join another pair and compare reasons.
Look at the results
Show the totals. Groups describe what was most and least popular and suggest why. Ask whether the result surprised them.
Report one thing
Each group prepares a sentence about the results. Hear a few, then ask partners to share an opinion they hadn’t expected.
frames: “Most of us chose ___.” · “___ is more popular than ___.” · “I chose ___ because ___.”
skills: Comparing amounts · Reporting a class result · Explaining a preference
support: Use “More students chose ___ than ___.”
stretch: Estimate the proportion choosing each option and predict another class’s result.

rounds.title: What is the best way to start the school day?
Which class trip would you choose?
Which new club would you try?

note: The vote only takes a minute. Leave most of the time for the reasons behind it.

title: Story Chain
purpose: Build a story round the group, one sentence at a time. Each person has to listen before adding their part.
setup: Groups sit where they can hear each other. Show an opening line. They can tell the story aloud; the box on the page is there for a shared class example.
steps: Start a story
Read the opening and add one sentence. Explain that each new sentence needs to connect to what came before.
Go round twice
Everyone adds a sentence in turn. Keep going for two rounds. Help with a missing word if someone gets stuck.
Add a problem
Reveal the extra detail and continue the story. Go round again, then decide how it ends. Practise a short retelling.
Tell it to someone else
Groups retell the story to their neighbours. Listeners identify the problem and a detail they remember.
frames: “Then ___.” · “But suddenly ___.” · “Because of that, ___.” · “In the end, ___.”
skills: Listening to other speakers · Linking sentences · Telling a story
support: Keep then, because and finally on the board.
stretch: Make each speaker refer to a detail from the previous sentence.

rounds.title: I picked up the wrong schoolbag this morning.
rounds.answer: There is a note inside, addressed to you.

rounds.title: This morning, every clock in the city stopped.
rounds.answer: One student’s watch still works.

rounds.title: The bus stopped, but nobody got on or off.
rounds.answer: The driver is looking for someone in the queue.

note: Watch for one confident student taking over the plot. Give everyone a turn, even if they only add a short sentence.

title: Speed Chat
purpose: Short conversations with a few different classmates. The follow-up question is what keeps each one going.
setup: Arrange pairs and decide how partners will change. Use the one-minute timer for each person’s turn. Students can choose another question if they prefer.
steps: Show a short exchange
Answer a question, ask “Why?” or “How about you?”, and respond. Make clear that both partners need a turn.
Talk, then change partners
Show a question and give each person about a minute. Change partners and use the next question. Leave time to move.
Try two more questions
Continue with new partners. Ask each student to add a follow-up question before sharing their own answer.
Remember an idea
Students tell a partner an interesting idea they heard. Ask which follow-up question got a longer answer.
frames: “What do you like about ___?” · “Why is that?” · “How about you?”
skills: Taking turns · Asking follow-up questions · Listening for detail
support: Show the next question early and let students plan a few words.
stretch: Ask two follow-up questions before giving your own answer.

rounds.title: What small thing makes a school day better?
rounds.answer: Why does it make a difference?

rounds.title: What skill would you like to learn?
rounds.answer: Who could help you start?

rounds.title: If you could invent a new snack, what would it be?
rounds.answer: What would you call it?

rounds.title: Where would you go with one free afternoon?
rounds.answer: What would you do there?

rounds.title: What makes a good teammate?
rounds.answer: Can you give an example?

note: If answers stop after one word, model a follow-up. “Why?” is often enough.

title: Category Sprint
purpose: Teams list words in a category for one minute, then explain a few of the words they chose.
setup: Each team needs paper. Show a category and use the one-minute timer. The word box on the page can collect a shared class list afterwards.
steps: Check the category
Give two examples and explain that repeated words only count once. Students need to know what their words mean.
Make a list
Give teams a minute to write as many words as they can. Then each person explains one entry to the group.
Try another category
Repeat with a new category. Teams choose three useful words and put each into a sentence. Everyone contributes.
Keep a few words
Take a word and an explanation from each team. Partners choose one word to remember and use it in a sentence.
frames: “___ belongs because ___.” · “It means ___.” · “You can use it to ___.”
skills: Recalling vocabulary · Explaining word meanings · Using words in sentences
support: Give two starter words and allow students to sketch before naming an object.
stretch: Ask for an explanation in English before accepting a word.

rounds.title: Things you can find in a kitchen
rounds.answer: Choose three words and explain what each thing is used for.

rounds.title: Things that can move
rounds.answer: Choose three words and describe how they move.

rounds.title: Words to describe a good friend
rounds.answer: Choose three words and give an example of each.

rounds.title: Things to pack for a trip
rounds.answer: Choose three words and say why you need those things.

note: A long list is fine, but check that they can actually use the words. Spend time on two or three good examples.

title: Sentence Detective
purpose: Find what needs changing in a sentence, agree on a better version and explain the change.
setup: Show one sentence at a time. Pairs use paper to write a correction. Leave the suggested answer hidden until they have had a go.
steps: Find a clue
Read the sentence and ask what they notice. Point to a time word or a subject if they need a place to start.
Compare corrections
Pairs write a new version and explain their choice. Reveal the suggested answer and compare.
Try a few more
Work through the next sentences. Join another pair to discuss before revealing. If there is time, write a simple puzzle for the other pair.
Explain one change
Each student explains a correction to a partner. Take two examples and repeat the useful sentence pattern.
frames: “We changed ___ to ___ because ___.” · “The clue is ___.”
skills: Reading carefully · Correcting sentences · Explaining a change
support: Offer two corrected versions to choose from.
stretch: Find another correct way to express the same meaning.

rounds.title: Yesterday I go to the park.
rounds.answer: Yesterday I went to the park. “Yesterday” points to a finished past action.

rounds.title: She don’t like bananas.
rounds.answer: She doesn’t like bananas. Use “doesn’t” with he, she or it in the present simple.

rounds.title: Where you live?
rounds.answer: Where do you live? This present simple question needs “do” before “you”.

rounds.title: There is three books on the desk.
rounds.answer: There are three books on the desk. Use “are” with a plural noun.

rounds.title: My bag is more heavy than yours.
rounds.answer: My bag is heavier than yours. We usually say “heavier” when comparing how heavy two things are.

note: They don’t need the name of the grammar rule. Ask what changed and why it makes sense.

title: Word Connections
purpose: Link one word to the next and explain each connection. See where the group ends up.
setup: Show a starting word. Groups go round in order. Use the shared list for a class example, or let groups build their chains aloud.
steps: Show a connection
Try “Rain → umbrella, because it keeps you dry.” Make clear that they need a reason for the link.
Build a chain
Each person adds a word connected to the last one and explains why. Go round at least twice. Help each other when needed.
Aim somewhere
Start again and reveal the target word. Try to reach it in five links, explaining each step. Compare possible routes.
Share an unusual link
Groups share a connection that needed explaining. Partners retell part of their chain using because.
frames: “___ makes me think of ___ because ___.” · “They both ___.”
skills: Making word associations · Giving reasons · Following another speaker’s idea
support: Offer two possible words if someone gets stuck.
stretch: Reach the target in exactly five links without repeating a word.

rounds.title: Rain
rounds.answer: Target: music

rounds.title: School
rounds.answer: Target: ocean

rounds.title: Breakfast
rounds.answer: Target: adventure

rounds.title: A bicycle
rounds.answer: Target: a movie

note: There can be several good connections. Ask them to make the link clear to someone outside the group.
